title: Photographers
description: Photograph people, landscapes, merchandise, or other subjects. May use lighting equipment to enhance a subject's appearance. May use editing software to produce finished images and prints. Includes commercial and industrial photographers, scientific photographers, and photojournalists.
tasks: Adjust apertures, shutter speeds, and camera focus according to a combination of factors, such as lighting, field depth, subject motion, film type, and film speed.
Create artificial light, using flashes and reflectors.
Determine desired images and picture composition, selecting and adjusting subjects, equipment, and lighting to achieve desired effects.
Transfer photographs to computers for editing, archiving, and electronic transmission.
Use traditional or digital cameras, along with a variety of equipment, such as tripods, filters, and flash attachments.
Manipulate and enhance scanned or digital images to create desired effects, using computers and specialized software.
Take pictures of individuals, families, and small groups, either in studio or on location.
Enhance, retouch, and resize photographs and negatives, using airbrushing and other techniques.
Test equipment prior to use to ensure that it is in good working order.
Estimate or measure light levels, distances, and numbers of exposures needed, using measuring devices and formulas.
Perform general office duties, such as scheduling appointments, keeping books, and ordering supplies.
Review sets of photographs to select the best work.
Set up, mount, or install photographic equipment and cameras.
Determine project goals, locations, and equipment needs by studying assignments and consulting with clients or advertising staff.
Perform maintenance tasks necessary to keep equipment working properly.
Select and assemble equipment and required background properties, according to subjects, materials, and conditions.
Direct activities of workers setting up photographic equipment.
Engage in research to develop new photographic procedures and materials.
Mount, frame, laminate, or lacquer finished photographs.
Send film to photofinishing laboratories for processing.
Develop visual aids and charts for use in lectures or to present evidence in court.
Load and unload film.
Write photograph captions.
Set up photographic exhibitions for the purpose of displaying and selling work.
Produce computer-readable, digital images from film, using flatbed scanners and photofinishing laboratories.
Employ a variety of specialized photographic materials and techniques, including infrared and ultraviolet films, macro photography, photogrammetry and sensitometry.
License the use of photographs through stock photo agencies.
Develop and print exposed film, using chemicals, touch-up tools, and developing and printing equipment.

role_contexts.Face-to-Face Discussions with Individual: Once a week or more but not every day
role_contexts.Contact With Others: Contact with others most of the time

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to arrest a fleeting moment and make it permanently visible—to prove that what was seen actually existed and can be returned to.
psychological_profile.decision_style: They freeze when uncertain, gathering light readings, angles, and compositional options until the window closes, then act on accumulated visual intuition rather than consensus or data. Under pressure, they trust what the frame shows them in the viewfinder over what others describe.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They notice the quality and direction of light before faces or objects, registering shadows, color temperature, and reflected surfaces while often missing spoken instructions or social subtext happening in the same space.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: They withdraw into technical work—adjusting equipment, reviewing shots—using physical busyness to avoid verbal confrontation, then return with a finished image that argues their case silently. The emotional cost is accumulated isolation and late resentment.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: They accept physical and equipment risks (heights, weather, gear failure) but resist creative risks that might damage their visual reputation or client relationships; technical failure is honorable, aesthetic failure is not.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They orbit the group periphery with equipment as a legitimate reason for distance, becoming temporarily central only when directing subjects, then retreating. Unassigned, they default to observer—present but not participating in the interaction they document.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They negotiate hierarchies through technical expertise, offering irreplaceable visual skills as leverage rather than complying or resisting directly—authority is tolerated when it doesn't interfere with the decisive moment.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First, a visceral sense of having been robbed by time itself—of the moment that escaped. Then they obsessively review what was captured, searching salvageable frames rather than analyzing errors, often producing unexpected secondary value from 'ruined' shoots.
value_hierarchy: the decisive moment over comprehensive coverage
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They believe that seeing something through a lens makes them understand it, conflating visual capture with genuine comprehension of people and situations.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need to be invisible to capture authenticity, yet crave recognition for the vision only they could have produced from that invisibility.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not shoot without reviewing the frame themselves—delegating the viewfinder to another, even a client or director, feels like surrendering their nervous system.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat images as infinitely reproducible and therefore disposable, asking for 'just a few more shots' without understanding that each click depletes a finite reserve of authentic expression from the subject.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They distrust the professional virtue of enthusiastic collaboration and 'yes, and' energy, seeing it as the enemy of the critical distance and selective restraint that makes images powerful rather than merely agreeable.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When images fail, they blame the light—its absence, its betrayal, its refusal to cooperate—before considering their own timing, preparation, or technical choices.
